newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Looming drugs row could strain NZ-U.S. trade.
newsitem.headline: Looming drugs row could strain NZ-U.S. trade.

text.p: New Zealand's controversial pharmaceuticals subsidy policy could get it added to a U.S. exporters "priority watch list" this week, straining trade links between the two countries.
Big U.S. research-based drugmakers have asked their trade agency, the U.S. Trade Representative, to impose the watch list sanction on New Zealand.
They argue the practices of Pharmac, a state subsidy agency, deny them access to the New Zealand market.
"There is a valid case, no question about it," said Kim Miles, chief executive of the drugmakers' New Zealand lobby group the Researched Medicines Industry (RMI).
"Companies face delays in being able to get access into the New Zealand market because of some of the ways Pharmac operates," he said.

The U.S. Trade Representative is expected to issue its annual report on trade barriers on Wednesday. "Countries placed on the priority watch list are the focus of increased bilateral attention concerning the problem area of practice," it warned.
Miles said a priority watch listing could at best be a slap on the hand. At worst it could result in retaliation against New Zealand exporters to the United States.

"There could be some retaliation. If New Zealand was trying to get more favourable entry for something into the States, undoubtedly this question would sit on the table and would be discussed before anything we wanted was considered," he said.
The New Zealand pharmaceutical market is currently worth about NZ$729 million (US$506 million), of which the U.S. market share is around NZ$211 million, or 29 percent.
Pharmac's function is to select the medicines which receive government funds allocated to the national public health system.
U.S. drugmakers claim Pharmac will not subsidise a new medicine unless it is offered at a lower price than currently available competing medicines in the same class.
But Pharmac said it would stand firm on its purchasing policies, saying it would not be bullied by the giant U.S. pharmaceuticals industry.
"We subsidise medicines for New Zealanders, not subsidise American drug companies for their shareholders," Pharmac general manager David Moore told Reuters.
"Their (U.S. drug companies') official complaint is simply driven by commercial concerns that Pharmac is beginning to force suppliers to compete for subsidy."

He said some of Pharmac's policies were "leading edge" and he suspected the drug companies were afraid of a domino effect happening internationally. "There's some fear of other countries picking up what we're doing," he said.
"For instance, British Columbia has adopted some of the same techniques for managing pharmaceuticals, and the Australians are looking at it."
Drugmakers fear a system that would prevent them from achieving significant sales of a prescription drug in New Zealand unless it is subsidised.

"Effectively, no product is sold unless it is subsidised because obviously, as a patient, you're not going to want to pay $100 for a prescription when there's something else that you only pay your standard prescription charge for," Miles said.
New Zealanders pay a basic charge of NZ$15 per subsidised prescription, NZ$3 if they on state benefits, but the total cost can vary depending on the medicine and quantity. (US$1 = NZ$1.44)
